Read the Interface, Not the File: How ASL Outline and Symbol Queries Keep Agent Context Sharp

2026-09-01Context Architecture5 min read

These notes were written in September 2026, before the C host was removed, and describe designs as well as shipped behaviour. Where a post says asl-host check or asl-host test, the command today is asl check or asl test; ERR_READ_UNBALANCED is now ERR_UNBALANCED; and the current checker does not reject an unmarked effect (ERR_EFFECT_UNMARKED). Figures are the ones measured on the date each post gives. Current docs

By GenSEAM | September 2026

When an agent works in an AgentSlang (ASL) repository, it does not dump whole files into its prompt to learn how a module works. In one batched toolbelt call, (:intel :op outline :file ...) and (:read :file ... :symbol ...) return just the exported signatures and the exact definition the task touches, while the checker's module headers (:x [...]) state explicitly what is public.

That directly prevents the failure mode that stalls multi-agent swarms on large codebases: Context Rot. When a coordinator injects full source files into subagent prompts, working memory fills with private implementation details, attention drifts, and subagents start calling internal helpers or misquoting signatures.

Feeding an agent only the interface and the symbols it edits keeps prompts small and boundaries clear. Below we show how ASL's interface extraction works and measure the reduction on a representative module.

1. The Anatomy of Context Rot in Multi-Agent Swarms

When a model's context window is flooded with raw implementation details across many modules:

  1. Lost in the Middle: Models attend most reliably to the beginning and the end of a long prompt; interface contracts defined in files placed in the middle are easier to overlook.
  2. Scope Leakage and Identifier Hallucination: When an agent sees hundreds of lines of private helpers (_internal_sort, _format_buffer), it starts calling them instead of programming to the public API.
  3. Latency: Prompt ingestion time grows with prompt length, and in a swarm where agents call one another, that overhead is paid on every hop.

The caller agent does not care how a module computes tax or serializes a buffer; it only needs to know what types it accepts, what it returns, and what guarantees it holds.

2. AST Interface Extraction: Compressing Implementation to Contract

An AgentSlang (ASL) module declares its public surface in its header: :x lists the exported names. That makes the interface a property of the syntax tree rather than a convention.

Consider an order module (124 tokens under cl100k_base):

(module store/orders :x [calculateTotal] :i [])

enum OrderStatus (pending) (completed txId: String)

schema Order
  id: Int64
  total: Float64

fn regionalTaxMultiplier rate: Float64 -> Float64
  (+ 1.0 (/ rate 100.0))

fn calculateTotal items: (List Order) taxRate: Float64 -> Float64
  (let [(subtotal (fold (fn [acc o] (+ acc o.total)) 0.0 items))
        (multiplier (regionalTaxMultiplier taxRate))]
    (* subtotal multiplier))

A peer subagent that only needs to build orders and ask for totals can receive the interface instead (64 tokens):

(module store/orders :x [calculateTotal] :i [])

enum OrderStatus (pending) (completed txId: String)

schema Order
  id: Int64
  total: Float64

fn calculateTotal items: (List Order) taxRate: Float64 -> Float64
  0.0

Both files pass asl check. On this one module the interface is 48.4% smaller under cl100k_base (124 to 64 tokens; 123 to 64, 48.0%, under o200k_base), counted with js-tiktoken 1.0.15 on 2026-10-14 over each file as checked. A single module is an illustration, not a repository-wide figure.

Why Naive Stripping Fails: The Valid Stub Rule

Regex or header-only truncation often emits files that no longer parse. In ASL a function header is followed by an indented body, so an extractor that drops the body without replacing it leaves broken syntax that downstream tools cannot analyse.

An extractor that works on the syntax tree avoids this:

  • It drops private top-level functions (here regionalTaxMultiplier, which is not in :x).
  • For exported functions it keeps the name, the typed parameters and the return type (-> Type), and it can carry their doc rows from the package doc.asn, where ASL keeps documentation out of the source.
  • It replaces each body with a type-satisfying default (0.0 for Float64, 0 for Int64, "" for String).

The result is not a text fragment but a module the checker accepts.

What exists today: the (:intel :op outline :file "...") operation returns each top-level item of a file with its kind, signature and export flag. The step that renders that outline back into a checkable stub module is what we are building next.

3. Measuring the Saving

The saving that matters is repository-wide: full-source handoffs against interface handoffs, over many modules, with the tokenizer, the task set and the date stated, plus a downstream measure of whether subagents call fewer private or nonexistent names. We have not run that benchmark yet, so this post quotes no repository-wide percentage, latency, or hallucination rate.

4. Keeping Semantics Under Composition

Token savings are worthless if they cause regressions. Three properties keep a subagent honest when it writes against a stub:

  1. Checked Names, Arity and Types: asl check rejects an unknown name (ERR_UNKNOWN_SYMBOL), a call with the wrong number of arguments (ERR_ARITY) and an argument of the wrong declared type (ERR_TYPE_MISMATCH, for example a String passed where an Int64 is declared) before anything runs.
  2. Contract-Carrying Docs: Handing over the doc rows of the exported names keeps units (for example a :timeoutMs field) and preconditions in front of the subagent.
  3. Hermetic Boundaries: A private helper is absent from the stub, so a subagent cannot depend on it by reading about it.

Summary

Context engineering is not about fitting bigger files into bigger windows. It is about the information density of every token sent. Making interface extraction a first-class operation on the syntax tree is how AgentSlang intends to cut the token tax; the single-module figure above shows the mechanism, and the repository-wide benchmark will show its size.
